title: The Strategic Art of Workforce Segmentation and How to Put It to Work
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that what most organisations call workforce segmentation (cutting engagement data by grade, gender, tenure or location) is really demographic categorisation, and that genuine segmentation is a multi-dimensional discipline borrowed from consumer market research. He lays out a spectrum running from demographic through role-based to attitudinal and psychographic segmentation, placing the greatest strategic value at the psychographic end, where employees are grouped by what they value and why they work. The article's key move is to locate failure less in method than in use. Organisations pick the wrong lens for the question (describing who is leaving rather than why), produce rich segment insight and then apply one generic intervention to everyone, or treat a segmentation model as a one-off exercise that goes stale. Karian recommends pairing a structural lens with a motivational or behavioural one, translating segments into differentiated onboarding, development and retention approaches within privacy limits, and refreshing models every two to three years while validating them against outcomes.
points: Employees with identical demographic profiles can be driven by purpose, security, progression or social connection, so a single employee value proposition cannot serve all of them.
Role-based segmentation by criticality, skills adjacency and automation risk answers workforce-planning questions that demographic cuts cannot.
Combining a structural lens with a motivational or behavioural lens turns a description of a problem (who is leaving) into an explanation (why they leave and what would retain them).

The biggest failure is operational: organisations build sophisticated segment models and then apply a generic intervention to every segment, unlike consumer functions that have differentiated for decades.
Segmentation should be a living model refreshed every two to three years, and a failed intervention should prompt the question of whether the segment was accurately characterised.
quotes: They produce a slide that shows that managers are more satisfied than individual contributors, and that people in their first-year rate their onboarding lower than those who have been around longer. Sadly, this is simply demographic categorisation with a more impressive name.

Getting it right is one of the highest-value things an HR or people analytics function can do. Getting it wrong is largely invisible. Organisations that segment badly simply never know what they’re missing.

Research across multiple industries consistently shows that employees with identical demographic profiles (same age, same role, same tenure) can have fundamentally different relationships with work: some driven by purpose and contribution, others by financial security, others by career progression, others by social connection. A single EVP cannot effectively serve all four simultaneously.

That finding is real but it doesn’t tell you why they’re leaving, what would have retained them, or what interventions will change the pattern. Layering attitudinal data (from survey responses, exit interviews, and focus groups) onto the demographic substrate turns a description into an explanation.
The most significant failure mode in workforce segmentation is not methodological. It is operational.

This simply reflects the kind of segmentation that consumer-facing functions have been doing it for decades. The reluctance to apply the same rigour to internal audiences is one of the more curious features of organisational life.
A segmentation model built on 2022 survey data, applied to 2025 workforce decisions, is a historical document with an unjustified air of authority.

The two questions lead to very different next steps. The discipline of asking both is what separates organisations that improve over time from those that conduct segmentation exercises and file the outputs.
